phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], plain and unaspirated, as in English 'spark'; Old Norse initial s never weakens.
Short close front unrounded [i], clipped brief — the short i of Old Norse, never the long í.
Nasal [n] plus the epenthetic stop [d] that Old Norse grew between n and r, then trilled or tapped [r] — the cluster the runes write with t.
Final short [i], fully sounded — Old Norse masculine -i names end in a true vowel, not a schwa.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SIN-dri' — two short beats, the weight on the first, the d clicked crisply between the n and the r as in 'laundry' said fast, both vowels clipped.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Sindri, brother of Brokkr and maker of Gullinbursti, Draupnir, and Mjǫllnir; beside the verb sindra, 'to sparkle, throw off sparks', and sindr, 'forge-slag, sparks'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᛁᚾᛏᚱᛁ (s-i-n-t-r-i), the Viking-Age runic rendering; the short-twig row writes the n-d-r cluster with its undifferentiated stop rune.

kin.label: Manuscript variant
kin.form: Eitri — part of the manuscript tradition of Skáldskaparmál names Brokkr's brother thus, and the handbooks treat Sindri and Eitri as one smith.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Sindri, an unbroken living male given name in Iceland, still carrying the forge's spark.

pronunciation.note: Sindri is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The smith whose name means 'sparkling' leaves his mark in meaning, not in orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf Smith
domains.subtitle: The Forge of the Three Treasures
domains.lead: Sindri is the dwarf at the anvil while his brother [[brokkr|Brokkr]] works the bellows: the smith who took Loki's wager and cast, in three heats, the golden-bristled boar Gullinbursti for Freyr, the ring Draupnir for Óðinn, and the hammer Mjǫllnir for Þórr — the greatest single afternoon's work in the northern corpus, done to win a bet staked on a trickster's head. His name is his trade: sindra, 'to sparkle', the forge-word for metal throwing off sparks. And Völuspá gives him a second life beyond Snorri's forge-scene: north on Niðavellir stands a hall of gold belonging to the kindred of Sindri, a dwarf chieftain of the verse tradition whose family owns the golden house.

cards.name: The Bellows That Must Not Stop
cards.desc: Brokkr's station and the wager's condition: the bellows must blow without pause through each casting, and the one moment they faltered — a fly's sting between the eyes — shortened the hammer's handle forever.

cards.name: Gullinbursti
cards.desc: The boar with bristles of gold, cast from a pigskin in the first heat and given to Freyr — Gold-Bristle, who runs through sky and sea faster than any horse and lights the darkest night with his shining mane.

cards.name: Draupnir
cards.desc: The gold arm-ring cast in the second heat and given to Óðinn — the Dripper, from which eight rings of equal weight drop every ninth night; Óðinn laid it on Baldr's pyre, and Baldr sent it back from Hel.

cards.name: Mjǫllnir the Short-Handled
cards.desc: The hammer cast in the third heat and given to Þórr — it never misses, never breaks, and always returns to the hand, yet its handle is a finger too short: the one flaw in the corpus's greatest treasure, made by an interrupted bellows-stroke.

symbols.name: The bellows
symbols.meaning: The wager's condition and the forge's heartbeat — the one tool whose failure, for a single instant, marks the hammer forever

symbols.name: The fly that stung
symbols.meaning: Loki's sabotage in miniature — the god who cannot win the contest fairly trying to spoil the work, and succeeding only at the handle

symbols.name: Draupnir
symbols.meaning: The ring that drips eight rings every ninth night — wealth that renews itself, the forge's answer to Andvari's cursed gold

symbols.name: Mjǫllnir's short handle
symbols.meaning: The flaw in perfection — the Æsir's best defense carries the permanent mark of the moment the work was broken

symbols.name: The golden hall at Niðavellir
symbols.meaning: Völuspá's witness — the house of gold of Sindri's kindred in the dwarf-fields, a chieftain's seat beyond Snorri's forge-scene

mythology.lead: Sindri's dossier is one long scene in Snorri and one stanza in Völuspá — a forge and a hall. The Prose Edda gives him the wager that produced the gods' three greatest treasures; the Poetic Edda gives him a golden house in the dwarf-fields and a kindred to fill it. Between the two stands the corpus's most consequential craftsman: everything the Æsir trust in the last battle came off his anvil in a single afternoon.

myths.title: The Wager of the Head
myths.text:
It begins with a crime: Loki, for mischief, cuts off all the hair of Sif, Þórr's wife. Þórr seizes him and would break every bone, and Loki swears to get the svartálfar to make hair of gold for Sif that will grow like living hair. He goes first to the sons of Ívaldi, who make the golden hair and two more treasures — the ship Skíðblaðnir for Freyr and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then, flushed with success, Loki goes to the dwarf Brokkr and wagers his own head that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three treasures just as good.

The bet is the whole engine of the chapter: a trickster's tongue staked against a smith's hands. Brokkr accepts, and the brothers go to the forge with the terms set — Sindri lays the metal, Brokkr works the bellows, and the bellows must not stop blowing until the work comes out of the fire.

myths.title: Three Castings, Three Stings
myths.text:
Sindri lays a pigskin in the forge and tells Brokkr to blow and never cease. A fly settles on Brokkr's hand and stings, but the bellows do not stop: out comes a boar with bristles of gold, Gullinbursti. Next Sindri lays gold in the fire; the fly returns and stings Brokkr's neck, harder, but the bellows do not stop: out comes the gold ring Draupnir. Last Sindri lays iron in the fire — and now, Snorri says, the smith himself fears the work will fail if the blowing falters. The fly settles between Brokkr's eyes and stings the eyelids so the blood runs down and blinds him; Brokkr sweeps the fly away with his hand, and the bellows fall silent for one instant. When the iron comes out it is a hammer — and its handle is short by a finger's breadth.

The fly, of course, is Loki, who cannot win the wager fairly and tries to spoil it instead. The chapter's precision is unforgettable: two perfect treasures and one marred, and the marred one — the hammer Mjǫllnir — is the greatest of the six. The sabotage succeeds exactly as far as the handle and no farther.

myths.title: The Judgment and the Sewn Lips
myths.text:
The brothers bring their three treasures to Ásgarðr, and the Æsir sit in judgment with Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr as assessors. To Freyr goes the boar, which runs through air and sea faster than any horse and lights the night with its golden bristles; to Óðinn the ring, which drips eight rings of equal weight every ninth night; to Þórr the hammer — it never misses what he throws at, it never breaks, it always returns to his hand, and it shrinks small enough to carry inside his shirt. Its one fault is the short handle. The judgment is unanimous: the hammer is the best of all the treasures, the surest defense against the frost-giants, and the brothers have won the wager.

Loki offers to ransom his head, but Brokkr refuses every price. When Loki tries to flee on his sky-shoes, Þórr catches him. Then comes the trickster's last legalism: the head was staked, but not one inch of the neck. Brokkr cannot take the head without touching the neck — so he takes an awl instead and sews Loki's lips together, and the thread, Snorri says, is called Vartari. The smith does not get his stake; he gets something better, the silencing of the tongue that staked it.

myths.title: The Golden Hall at Niðavellir
myths.text:
The verse tradition knows a grander Sindri than Snorri's forge-hand. Völuspá, in its survey of the world's dwellings, counts a hall that stands north on Niðavellir, made of gold, belonging to the kindred of Sindri — beside the giant Brimir's beer-hall at Ókólnir. Here Sindri is no lone craftsman but a dwarf chieftain, the head of a family rich enough to roof its house in the metal his name throws off as sparks.

The dwarf þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál keep the name in the catalogues of dwarf heiti, and the manuscript tradition splits on the forge-scene itself: where part of the tradition names Brokkr's brother Sindri, another part calls him Eitri, and the handbooks read the two as one smith under two forge-names. The name itself is the trade: sindra is 'to sparkle, throw off sparks', sindr is the slag and spark of the forge — kin to Old English sinder and the modern English cinder, the cooled spark of the smith's fire.

lore.syncretism: Sindri's closest kin are inside the corpus itself. His brother [[brokkr|Brokkr]] is the other half of one workshop — the two are never separated in the sources, bellows and anvil, and Snorri names the forge by the pair. [[andvari|Andvari]] is the corpus's other great dwarf of the gold, but inverted: Andvari's hoard is won by robbery and carries a curse, Sindri's gold is made in three heats and carries only a wager. Vǫlundr of Vǫlundarkviða, 'prince of elves', is the verse tradition's other smith narrative — the smith wronged who takes revenge, where Sindri is the smith wagered against who wins. Cross-culturally the comparisons are structural, not borrowed: Hephaistos, the Greek smith who forges the gods' masterworks and is himself marred; Ilmarinen of the Kalevala, who forges the Sampo under a bargain's pressure; Goibniu of the Irish Tuatha Dé Danann, whose smith-work arms the gods for their last battle. The pattern is old — the divine weapon must come from an other-than-divine hand — but Sindri's version is the only one where the masterpiece's flaw is timed to a single held breath of the bellows.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sindri's afterlife is the afterlife of his three treasures: every retelling of Norse myth that reaches the forging of Mjǫllnir keeps his one afternoon and its three stings, from the Victorian handbooks onward — the short handle is the detail no adapter has ever dared to cut, because it is the story. The smith himself has had a quieter reception than his work, and much of it flows under his manuscript double: the variant name Eitri carries the same dwarf-smith into a robust modern afterlife in games and film, where the forge that made the hammer is restaged for new audiences — the inventions are modern, but the forge, the brother, and the interrupted casting are Skáldskaparmál's own. The sturdiest legacy is the name: Sindri never died out in Iceland and remains a living male given name, borne today by men who inherit the forge's spark in its plainest form.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sindri is the Edda's shortest sermon on how perfection fails. The gods' three greatest treasures are made in one afternoon by a smith whose name is a forge-word for sparks, and two of them are flawless. The third — the best, the one the Æsir will trust in the last battle — is marred by a single instant: a fly, an eyelid, a held breath of the bellows, and the handle is short forever. The tradition does not call the hammer ruined; it calls it the finest thing ever forged, short handle and all. That is the forge's verdict and the story's mercy: the masterpiece is not the work that never faltered but the work that survived its interruption. Loki wins the sting and loses the wager. Sindri wins everything except the head he was promised — and takes the trickster's voice instead, one stitch at a time, with an awl. In a mythology that ends in fire, the smith who arms the gods gets the corpus's most practical blessing: his work holds, and no one remembers the fly who won.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Sindri — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᛁᚾᛏᚱᛁ (s-i-n-t-r-i), a normalized phonetic reconstruction in which the short-twig row writes the n-d-r cluster with its undifferentiated stop rune. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: sindri.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Sindri is a wholly textual dwarf: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no image can be securely identified with him. His attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses — the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for Skáldskaparmál 35 (with the Codex Upsaliensis tradition reading the brother's name as Eitri), and the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Völuspá's golden hall at Niðavellir. The material context is nonetheless richer for him than for most dwarfs, because his products are findable. Thor's-hammer pendants — Mjǫllnir in miniature — are the commonest amulets of the late Viking Age, known by the hundred from tenth-century graves, hoards, and settlement sites across Scandinavia and the diaspora: the forge's most famous casting, worn at the neck of the converted and unconverted alike. Gold arm-rings of Draupnir's type fill the hoards. And the corpus's visual language of the smithy survives on the Gotland picture stones — Ardre VIII shows a smithy scene with tools and a headless body, usually read as Vǫlundr — proof that the smith at his forge was a carved subject in the Viking-Age north, though no carving names Sindri himself.
